heuristics.condition: When a couple is in conflict and trying to resolve a substantive issue...
heuristics.action: ...restore emotional safety and reconnect first before introducing the topic to be solved
heuristics.because: Without emotional safety, the thinking brain is inaccessible, so any proposed solution will fail regardless of its quality

heuristics.rule: Distinguish the source of pain before deciding whether to repair or leave
heuristics.condition: When a partner is feeling relationship pain and is unsure whether to stay or go...
heuristics.action: ...ask whether the pain comes from what is missing (depletion) or from what has been done (breakage), and use that answer as the first fork in the decision
heuristics.because: Depleted relationships lack fuel but retain structural integrity; broken relationships have fractured foundations that require a different — often irrecoverable — kind of work

heuristics.rule: Treat contempt as a categorically different signal from ordinary conflict
heuristics.condition: When assessing whether a couple's negative patterns are repairable...
heuristics.action: ...check specifically for contempt rather than just frequency or intensity of conflict; if contempt has replaced conflict, treat this as a 'let go' indicator
heuristics.because: Contempt specifically predicts relationship failure in a way that other conflict behaviors do not

heuristics.rule: Require both partners' willingness as a minimum condition before recommending repair
heuristics.condition: When one partner is doing all the repair work and the other is not engaged...
heuristics.action: ...treat asymmetric effort as a hard stop on the repair path rather than a problem to be solved through more effort by the willing partner
heuristics.because: Repair requires two participants; sustained unilateral effort without reciprocation is a structural condition, not a temporary gap

heuristics.rule: Apply abuse as a hard override that pre-empts the depleted/broken diagnostic framework entirely
heuristics.condition: When any form of active abuse is present — physical, emotional, financial, or sexual...
heuristics.action: ...exit the diagnostic framework and treat leaving as the indicated path before running any other analysis
heuristics.because: Abuse is not a repair problem; running a repairability diagnosis in an abuse context delays safety and implicitly treats a safety issue as a relationship-quality issue

decision_factors.why_it_matters: If a person does not feel safe with their partner even when angry, the foundational condition for repair is absent and the relationship is more likely broken than depleted
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask directly: 'Do I still feel safe with this person, even when I am angry?' A yes suggests depletion is possible; a no points toward breakage

decision_factors.factor: Desire for the partner at their best
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Whether a person still wants the partner when they imagine them performing at their best separates exhaustion from the current version of the partner from a deeper loss of desire for the relationship itself
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: 'When I imagine my partner at their best, do I still want that person?' Persistent no indicates structural incompatibility rather than situational depletion

decision_factors.factor: Source of pain — missing vs. done
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Pain from what is missing signals depletion and points toward repair; pain from what has been done signals breakage and points toward leaving or a fundamentally different kind of work
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: 'Is the pain from what's missing or from what's been done?' and probe for specific incidents of betrayal, contempt, or abuse versus absence of positive experience

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Repair requires both partners to engage; if even one partner lacks willingness, the repair path is structurally blocked regardless of the other's effort or desire
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess whether both partners are actively pursuing help, not just one; look for asymmetric effort as the key signal

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Active abuse of any type — physical, emotional, financial, or sexual — overrides all other diagnostic factors and makes leaving the indicated path
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Screen explicitly for all four abuse types before entering any other diagnostic step; do not assume absence without checking

decision_factors.factor: Presence of contempt in conflict patterns
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Contempt specifically predicts relationship failure in a way that intensity or frequency of conflict alone does not; it signals a different quality of damage
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Distinguish whether the couple is in conflict (fighting about things) versus expressing contempt (communicating fundamental disrespect or disgust toward the person)

decision_factors.factor: Ratio of good years to bad years
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A history in which the good years outweigh the bad is cited as a condition supporting the decision to fight for the relationship; it establishes that positive relational structure existed and can potentially be restored
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the person to characterize the overall arc of the relationship — was the current state preceded by a long period of genuine wellbeing or has difficulty been the dominant pattern

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Fundamental incompatibility in core values is listed as an explicit 'let go' criterion, meaning it cannot be repaired through process or effort alone
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Examine whether the partners' foundational values — not preferences or habits — are in conflict; surface-level differences that stem from depletion behave differently from genuine values misalignment

decision_factors.factor: External life stressors as the primary cause of exhaustion
decision_factors.why_it_matters: When exhaustion originates from external stressors rather than from the relationship itself, the structural relationship may be intact and repair through reconnection is more viable
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Probe the timeline: did the deterioration begin coinciding with an identifiable external stressor, or did it arise from within the relationship dynamic itself

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Jumping straight to problem-solving during conflict
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The cognitive capacity required to use a proposed solution is unavailable when emotional safety is absent, so the conversation produces the appearance of effort without any functional progress and often increases resentment
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Analytically-oriented partners who default to solution-mode and mistake articulating a solution for doing the relational work

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Continuing to do unilateral repair work when a partner is unwilling
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Sustained effort by one partner in the absence of reciprocation can mask the structural condition — one partner's non-willingness — and delay recognition that the repair path is blocked, extending the period of loss before a decision is made
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: The more invested partner, particularly those with attachment patterns that orient toward working harder when a partner withdraws

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Running the depleted/broken diagnostic framework when abuse is present
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Framing abuse as a repairability question reframes a safety issue as a relationship-quality issue, which legitimizes continued exposure and misallocates the person's cognitive and emotional resources toward repair instead of exit
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People in emotionally abusive relationships where the damage is less visually obvious than physical abuse and is therefore more susceptible to being mislabeled as 'a rough patch'

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting for feelings of love to return before deciding to invest in repair
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: In depleted relationships, the absence of felt love is a symptom of the depletion, not evidence of broken foundations; waiting for love to return before acting means waiting for the outcome of the intervention before doing the intervention
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Partners who treat emotional states as diagnostic data rather than as a product of relational conditions that can be changed

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating a depleted relationship as broken and exiting prematurely
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Exhaustion from external stressors produces feelings indistinguishable from relationship-level damage; without a diagnostic framework, people mistake the symptom — absence of energy and warmth — for the condition — fractured foundations
failure_patterns.consequence: The person exits a structurally intact relationship that could have been restored, carrying the same unresolved stressors into the next relationship
warning_signs: Difficulty identifying specific incidents of betrayal or contempt when asked
Deterioration timeline correlates with a specific external stressor rather than an internal relational event

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating a broken relationship as merely depleted and attempting repair indefinitely
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Commitment, sunk-cost reasoning, or attachment to the historical version of the relationship makes it emotionally costly to apply the 'broken' label; the depleted framing is more hopeful and therefore preferred
failure_patterns.consequence: Sustained effort is invested in a repair process that cannot succeed because the structural conditions — abuse, contempt, values incompatibility, or unilateral willingness — have not changed
warning_signs: Repair attempts produce temporary relief but return to the same pattern
The person cannot answer 'yes' to the safety or best-self diagnostic questions but continues to frame the problem as effort or technique

failure_patterns.pattern: Attempting to solve the substantive problem before restoring emotional safety
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Problem-solving feels productive and is a socially legible form of effort; emotional reconnection feels less concrete and is harder to initiate, especially mid-conflict
failure_patterns.consequence: Conversations about real issues fail repeatedly, reinforcing the belief that the problems are unsolvable, when the actual barrier is the sequencing of the conversation rather than the content
warning_signs: Couple reports having the same argument repeatedly without resolution
Both partners feel unheard despite both talking at length

failure_patterns.pattern: Using the depleted/broken framework when abuse is the actual condition
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Emotional and financial abuse in particular do not present as obviously as physical abuse; the person in the relationship may lack a clear reference frame for labeling the behavior as abuse and instead interprets it as relationship difficulty
failure_patterns.consequence: The person remains in an unsafe situation longer than necessary because the framework being applied treats the situation as a repair problem with a viable solution
warning_signs: The person reports feeling unsafe but then qualifies it as 'sometimes' or 'only when angry'
External warning-sign checklists (e.g., thehotline.org) would trigger but the person has not consulted them

diagnostic_questions.question: Do I still feel safe with this person, even when I am angry?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the foundational condition for repair — emotional safety — is present; a no answer points toward breakage rather than depletion
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Proceed to assess whether pain is sourced in what is missing versus what has been done
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Probe whether the unsafety involves any form of active abuse before proceeding; if yes, the repair framework does not apply

diagnostic_questions.question: When I imagine my partner at their best, do I still want that person?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the loss of desire is situational — tied to the current depleted state of the partner — or fundamental, meaning the person no longer wants the relationship even under ideal conditions
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: This supports the depleted framing; explore what external or internal conditions have suppressed access to that version of the partner
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This points toward fundamental incompatibility or irreversible erosion; explore whether contempt, values conflict, or prolonged breakage explains the loss

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the pain from what is missing or from what has been done?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The structural nature of the damage; missing-based pain indicates depletion, done-based pain indicates breakage through specific acts of betrayal, contempt, or harm
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If pain is from what has been done, identify the specific acts and assess whether they constitute abuse or contempt-level damage
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If pain is from what is missing, assess what specifically is absent and whether it was present before, supporting the depleted framing

diagnostic_questions.question: Are both partners willing to try, or is only one partner doing the repair work?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the structural condition for repair — bilateral willingness — is present; unilateral effort signals a blocked repair path regardless of the effort's quality
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If both are willing, assess whether both are actively pursuing help or only one
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If only one is willing, treat this as a 'let go' indicator rather than a problem to solve through increased effort

diagnostic_questions.question: Is there active abuse of any kind — physical, emotional, financial, or sexual?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the hard override condition is present; if yes, the depleted/broken diagnostic framework does not apply and the indicated path is safety planning and exit
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Exit the repair diagnostic entirely and redirect to safety resources
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Proceed with the depleted/broken framework beginning with the safety and best-self questions

diagnostic_questions.question: Has contempt replaced conflict in the relationship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the negative relational pattern has crossed from repairable conflict to contempt, which specifically predicts failure; this distinction carries more predictive weight than conflict intensity or frequency
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Treat as a 'let go' indicator; contempt signals a qualitatively different level of damage from ordinary conflict
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Assess the nature and pattern of conflict; high-conflict relationships with mutual respect may still be in the depleted category

diagnostic_questions.question: Do the good years outweigh the bad in the overall arc of the relationship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether there is an established history of positive relational functioning that supports the case for repair; a relationship that has been predominantly difficult has less evidence of restorable foundations
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: This supports the 'worth fighting for' framing; use as evidence that positive relational structure existed and may be recoverable
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Probe whether the current difficulty represents an anomaly or the dominant pattern, and whether the positive history the person is holding onto is accurate or idealized

industry_realities.common_belief: If a relationship feels broken, it is broken and should be exited
industry_realities.actual_reality: Relationships that feel broken are sometimes depleted — structurally intact but running on empty due to external stressors — and the subjective feeling of brokenness cannot reliably distinguish the two without a structured diagnostic
industry_realities.implication: Apply a structured diagnostic before using felt sense as the primary decision input; the feeling of brokenness is data, not a conclusion

industry_realities.common_belief: Talking through problems is the core mechanism of relationship repair
industry_realities.actual_reality: Substantive problem-solving requires cognitive access that is only available after emotional safety and connection have been established; problem-solving conversations held without those conditions in place will fail regardless of the quality of the proposed solution
industry_realities.implication: Sequence repair conversations in the correct order — safety first, then connection, then cognitive work, then problem-solving — rather than leading with the substantive issue

industry_realities.common_belief: Both people trying hard is sufficient for a relationship to be repaired
industry_realities.actual_reality: Effort is necessary but not sufficient; the presence of abuse, contempt, fundamental values incompatibility, or unilateral willingness are conditions that effort cannot overcome, and continuing to try in their presence is not repair but delay
industry_realities.implication: Assess structural conditions — the 'let go' criteria — before investing further in effort-based repair; if any hard condition is present, additional effort should not be the next step

industry_realities.common_belief: Conflict is a sign that a relationship is in serious trouble
industry_realities.actual_reality: Conflict and contempt are categorically different; conflict is a normal feature of relationships and does not predict failure, while contempt — which involves fundamental disrespect or disgust directed at the person — specifically predicts failure
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate conflict for the presence of contempt rather than treating conflict presence or intensity as the relevant variable

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Begins with the substantive presenting problem — the argument, the betrayal, the drift — and tries to solve or evaluate it directly
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Begins by determining whether the structural conditions for repair are present before engaging the content of the problem at all
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Engaging the content before assessing structural conditions wastes effort when a hard override — abuse, contempt, unilateral willingness — is present and would have pre-empted the content entirely

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Use of felt sense as diagnostic data
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats the person's subjective experience — 'it feels broken' or 'I don't feel love anymore' — as a conclusion about the relationship's status
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats felt sense as a symptom to be diagnosed; applies structured questions to determine whether the feeling reflects depletion, breakage, or an upstream condition like abuse
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Feelings of brokenness or lovelessness are common symptoms of both depleted and broken relationships; treating them as conclusions produces false positives and false negatives at significant cost to the person

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Moves to problem-solving as soon as the substantive issue is identified, treating emotional processing as a preliminary that can be skipped when the issues are urgent
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Follows the safety-connection-cognition-problem-solving sequence explicitly, understanding that skipping steps earlier in the sequence doesn't accelerate the process — it breaks it
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Couples who attempt problem-solving without emotional safety in place fail, which reinforces the belief that the problem is unsolvable rather than that the intervention was mis-sequenced

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Identification of the real decision variable
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Frames the stay-or-leave decision around love, history, and effort — all of which are present in both repairable and irreparable relationships
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Frames the decision around checkable structural conditions — bilateral willingness, absence of abuse, absence of contempt, values compatibility — which actually discriminate between the two cases
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Love, history, and effort are present in many relationships that should be exited and absent in some that could be repaired; using them as the primary decision variables produces systematically poor decisions

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Interprets the willing partner's continued effort as evidence that repair is viable and encourages more of it
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Identifies unilateral effort as a structural signal — not a temporary gap to be closed through more effort — and assesses whether the non-willing partner's lack of engagement is itself a 'let go' condition
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Encouraging more unilateral effort when the structural condition is one partner's unwillingness extends the period of loss and misallocates the willing partner's resources toward an outcome that the structural condition makes unavailable
